short: Protector Domesticus translates as «household guard». An honorary title in the Roman army from the 3rd century onwards, and from the 4th century as bodyguards of the first persons of the Empire. The title of protector dates back to the middle of the 3rd century, then it was used only as a title of honor or simply a title of domestic servant; this designation meant only that these men were attached to the imperial family (domus). Beginning under Diocletian, the term was used to refer to a small unit of the imperial court. In 346 the domestici appeared as a corps and formed two scholae, one of infantry and the other of cavalry, each consisting of 500 men and under the command of the comes domesticorum. Unlike the imperial guard (scholae palatinae), the protectores domestici were not intended to fight alongside the Emperor. In fact, they performed a variety of tasks: they accompanied the Emperor or senior officers, acted as communication and intelligence officers, and could also be sent to arrest or assassinate high-ranking officials. Ammianus Marcellinus, who was himself a protector domesticus, tells how his group was sent by Constantius II to Gaul to eliminate the usurper Silvanus in 355 AD.
history: Rome’s Empire became so large that in its later period the Emperor could not be everywhere at once. As such he appointed ‘Comites’, trusted, high-ranking military and administrative figures who ran certain parts of the Empire in his stead. ‘Comes’ – the singular - is Latin for ‘Companion’, used here in direct reference to the Companions of Alexander the Great, the most trusted lieutenants of the greatest military leader the world had yet seen (and someone all Roman Emperors aspired to be like). The Comites were the Emperor’s own inner circle, the leading officials of the Empire, wielding posts of myriad descriptions and reasonability, from the ‘Comes Britanniarum’, who was in charge of Roman Britain’s defence, to the ‘Comes Sacrae Vestis’ – master of the Emperor’s wardrobe!
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
